chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
title: Tone, microphone technique and playing too loud
summary: In Denmark teachers praised Caldwell's tone; he backs off the mike, and Dance cites Coltrane's loudness.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone

blocks.x: Yeah. You very seldom see an alto player use a metal mouthpiece. It's some reason why it is. It's (unintelligible). That's what happened when I was over there in Denmark with the concert. I was telling you about these people sitting around with the promoter, and they were all high class teachers, instructors in music and all, and they called me off after we played the set. They said, the people love that tone of yours, said, you're not -- your tone is so melodious, beautiful when you play a slow number, when you play a fast number, say, you're playing it like them (unintelligible). Said, but the tone is so effective. He says, it's not harsh, because (unintelligible) using mouthpieces.

And they get out in that microphones and blow like mad, and the mike is turned up. I always back away from the mike, and the tone -- they say, we love your tone, not only your playing, but your tone is so beautiful. (Unintelligible).
Well, I mean you might have a beautiful tone, but you can still mess it up by --
-- not paying attention to the microphone.

You know, Benny Goodman -- I didn't mean to interfere (unintelligible) let me use this, but he told me he went to hear Coltrane when he was at Birdland, and he said, I found it interesting. But, he said, it was so loud, he was playing with the bell on the mike the whole time. He said, I couldn't stand it. I left after about ten minutes.
Now, I -- I mean I heard him once in San Francisco, and there was no need to go in the club. It was a hot night, you stand on the sidewalk.

It was loud enough to hear, and then Elvin Jones was on the drums, you know, so damn loud, you could stand out there and hear it. That -- I mean that's -- you can't -- you know, there's no reason or excuse or anything to be offered for that loudness.
No, it isn't. That's what happened in Denmark.
I mean you could end, if you wanted, you could bring a number to a climax with very loud, but I mean this business of playing loud the whole time (unintelligible), that's stupid.
It is. Always -- what I always could listen, hear, just how much volume, how much tone,

pressure to put on it. And then when I'd back off (unintelligible), we could hear just how (unintelligible) sound, because it become too harsh, I'd back off again. Like it's a slow tune, I'd go up to the mike, then the subtone. You'd blow loud in everything, it's too -- it's colorless.
